topic: Shutter speed 1/1000 vs 1/15 vs 15 s: real motion-blur simulation where a 50 km/h car freezes, streaks, then vanishes
lines: This photo has a car in it. You just can't see it.
It's driving at fifty kilometers an hour.
At one thousandth of a second, it moves one point four centimeters.
At 1/1000 of a second, it moves 1.4 cm.
At one fifteenth, it moves almost a meter.
At 1/15, it moves almost a meter.
At fifteen seconds, it drives over two hundred meters.
At 15 seconds, it drives over 200 meters.
Each spot sees it for under two percent of the time.
Each spot sees it for under 2% of the time.
One second turns it into fog.
But that's fifteen thousand times more light. Almost fourteen stops.
But that's 15,000× more light. Almost 14 stops.
So stop down, or add an N D filter.
So stop down, or add an ND filter.
Shooting handheld? Stay faster than one over your focal length.
Shooting handheld? Stay faster than 1 / your focal length.
Slow down enough, and anything moving disappears.
Like the car in this photo.

youtube.title: This Photo Has a Car in It. You Can't See It.
youtube.description:
Same street, same 50 km/h car (13.9 m/s), three shutter speeds:
1/1000 s → it moves 1.4 cm: frozen.
1/15 s → it moves ~0.93 m: a streak.
15 s → it drives ~208 m, so each point on its path sees the 4 m car for under 2% of the exposure: it disappears.
Water does the same: exposures longer than about half a second turn running water into a white, fog-like sheet.
The catch: 15 s is 15,000× the light of 1/1000 s (~14 stops), so you stop down or use an ND filter. Handheld rule of thumb: shutter speed ≈ 1/focal length (50mm → 1/50 s).
Every frame is a real simulation: the camera averages thousands of sub-frames over the exposure.
Sources: Wikipedia "Shutter speed"; cameraby.com shutter-speed guide.
